passage:
I'm Jasleen. After final year, our trio split three ways. I got a placement in Bengaluru. Rajni met a guy from her office in Delhi and suddenly had plans every weekend. Noor stayed back home and took tuition batches to help pay her brother's fees, so she was always tired.
At first we did Sunday video calls. Then every other Sunday. Then someone would cancel, usually me, because of a deadline. Now I mostly know Rajni's life through her posts. I like them. She likes mine.
Last month I saw her birthday photos and realised I hadn't called. I felt sick with guilt.
Then Rajni messaged: "Sorry I've gone missing, I keep meaning to call you." She felt it too. Neither of us had stopped caring. We just both kept waiting to be the one with free time.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen get a placement?
qa.a: Jasleen got a placement in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What did Jasleen feel on seeing Rajni's birthday photos, and why?
qa.a: Jasleen felt sick with guilt on realising there had been no call on Rajni's birthday.

qa.q: What could Jasleen and Rajni try so the friendship doesn't live only in likes?
qa.a: They could set a short, fixed call time that suits both schedules, or send voice notes, instead of waiting for free time that never comes.

qa.q: How is Rajni experiencing the same drift?
qa.a: Rajni feels guilty too: her message 'I keep meaning to call you' shows she still cares but is caught up in her new life.

grounding: Shows college friends scattering to a new city, a relationship and money struggles, with calls turning into likes and guilt on both sides.

passage:
Counselling note. Student: Rukmini, final year B.Com. Session 2.
Rukmini came in about placement stress, but most of the session was about her friends. Her group of three was very close through college. Now Aparna is in a relationship and busy most evenings, Deepa is working part-time because money is tight at home, and Rukmini has an offer in Chennai starting in July.
She showed me her phone: a string of hearts and "miss u" replies on Aparna's photos, and no real conversation in six weeks. "I keep thinking I should call. Then I think, she's the busy one, why should I always call?" Then, softer: "Maybe she's thinking the same about me."
She seemed relieved to say it aloud. We talked about how friends taking different paths is normal and not a verdict on the friendship. She plans to send Aparna a voice note tonight instead of another like. Will follow up next week.

qa.q: Where does Rukmini have an offer?
qa.a: Rukmini has an offer in Chennai starting in July.

qa.q: What is Rukmini feeling torn about as she looks at her phone?
qa.a: Rukmini feels she should call but resents always being the one to reach out, and then guesses Aparna may feel the same guilt.

qa.q: What step did Rukmini choose at this stage, and why might it help?
qa.a: Rukmini planned to send Aparna a voice note instead of another like; a real voice can reopen a conversation that likes cannot.

qa.q: How might Aparna be experiencing this gap?
qa.a: Aparna is busy with her relationship and may also feel guilty for not calling, waiting for Rukmini to make the first move.

grounding: Illustrates a friend group diverging through a relationship, money pressure and a new job city, with likes replacing calls and guilt on both sides.

passage:
So you want to know what happened to our gang? I'm Parveen, I was the loud one, I'll tell you.

Four of us, all through college. Then final year ended. Varun got placed in Chennai and suddenly worked till ten every night. Rukhsar fell in love and we saw her on weekends only if he was busy. And I was stuck at home, taking tuitions to help my father with the loans. I didn't want anyone to see how tight things were.

At first we did long video calls. Then short ones. Then just reacting to each other's posts. Heart. Laughing face. Heart.

Last month Varun messaged, "Sorry, I've been a terrible friend." And I wrote back, "No, I should have called." We both felt guilty, and we still didn't call.

It isn't anyone's fault. That's what makes it strange.

qa.q: Where did Varun get placed?
qa.a: In Chennai.

qa.q: How does Parveen feel about the calls turning into reactions on posts?
qa.a: Parveen feels guilty and sad, and also a little ashamed about the money trouble at home, which made reaching out harder.

qa.q: What could Parveen or Varun do next, instead of both apologising?
qa.a: One of them could suggest a specific time to talk, like a short call on Sunday, so the guilt turns into contact.

qa.q: What is it like for Varun, working till ten every night?
qa.a: He may be exhausted and feel guilty, like Parveen, and not know how to restart the friendship.

grounding: Parveen describes a college gang drifting apart through a job, a relationship and money struggles, with calls turning into likes and both feeling guilty for not calling.

passage:
July. Manoj and Santosh had lived one lane apart in Nashik since childhood. When Santosh left for his placement in Gurugram, they promised to call every Sunday. The first Sunday call lasted two hours.

October, three months later. Manoj's new relationship took his weekends; Santosh's project meant late nights. The calls became voice notes. The voice notes became reactions to each other's photos. When Santosh posted a picture of a new office, Manoj sent a thumbs up and felt a small pinch.

December, on the day Santosh came home for a wedding. They met at the old tea stall. Both started with "Sorry, I should have called," at the same moment, and laughed awkwardly.

On the walk back, Manoj realised they had talked for an hour about work and not once about anything real.

qa.q: Where did Manoj and Santosh meet in December?
qa.a: At the old tea stall.

qa.q: What does the "small pinch" Manoj feels at the office photo suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels a sting of guilt and sadness at how far apart they have grown, and a little left behind.

qa.q: What could they try now that both have apologised?
qa.a: They could agree on something small and specific, like a monthly call about more than work, instead of only promising to do better.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel saying "Sorry, I should have called"?
qa.a: He likely feels guilty too, sharing the same sense of being the one who let the calls fade.

grounding: Over three beats Manoj and Santosh drift as a placement and a relationship take over, calls become likes, and both feel guilty for not calling.

passage:
Shreya, you're worried because your college friends have scattered. Your old Farhan uncle has been through this, thirty years ago.

When I was your age there were three of us in Lucknow: me, Anil, and Rehana. Then everything happened at once. I got a job in Bombay. Anil fell for a girl and vanished into her family. Rehana's father fell ill, and she had to run his shop and had no time or money for trips.

We wrote letters at first. Then postcards. Then a line at New Year. Every New Year I thought, I should visit Rehana, and every year I didn't. I felt guilty, and I later learned she felt the same about me.

The turning point came when I finally took a train to Lucknow, unannounced. Rehana opened the door and burst out laughing.

qa.q: What did Rehana have to do after her father fell ill?
qa.a: Run his shop.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel every New Year when he didn't visit?
qa.a: Farhan felt guilty, and later learned Rehana felt guilty too.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Farhan finally took the train to Lucknow unannounced; it broke the cycle where both felt guilty but neither acted.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when she opened the door and saw Farhan?
qa.a: She probably felt surprised and delighted, and maybe relieved after years of her own guilt.

grounding: Farhan, an elder, tells Shreya how his college friends diverged through a job, a relationship and a family burden, and how both sides felt guilty for not calling.

passage:
The call dropped for the third time. Ganga was on the rooftop of her Bengaluru PG, the only place with signal, and it had started to drizzle.

Aparna's face froze on the screen, mid-sentence. Then: "Network weak."

It had been like this since college ended. Ganga had the placement in Bengaluru. Aparna had stayed in Jaipur and was working evenings at her uncle's shop because her family needed the money. Their third friend, Sonal, now only posted pictures with her boyfriend.

Once, they'd talked every night. Now it was hearts on each other's posts. Ganga had missed Aparna's birthday call by a whole day. Aparna hadn't asked about Ganga's new job.

Ganga typed, "Sorry, net's bad. Talk soon?" and felt guilty even as she sent it. She knew Aparna probably felt guilty too. Neither of them would say "soon" meant nothing.

qa.q: Where was Ganga's PG?
qa.a: Ganga's PG was in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she sent 'Talk soon?'
qa.a: She felt guilty, knowing the friendship was slipping and suspecting 'soon' might not happen.

qa.q: What small step could keep this friendship alive despite the distance?
qa.a: Ganga could suggest a fixed short call once a week at a time that fits Aparna's evening shifts, so they don't rely on chance.

qa.q: How might Aparna be experiencing the drift?
qa.a: Aparna is busy and under pressure at the shop, and likely also feels guilty for not asking about Ganga's job.

grounding: With poor signal and different lives, friends drift as calls turn into likes, and each feels guilty for not calling.
